question: What is the ServiceNow SDK (Now SDK) and Fluent, and when would you use it instead of App Engine Studio?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

They want to know you understand the modern, code-first way to build ServiceNow apps — the Now SDK and its declarative Fluent library — and that you can articulate when it beats clicking through App Engine Studio. Strong candidates frame it as source-control-first development, not a replacement for the platform.

The Answer

The ServiceNow SDK (Now SDK) lets you build a scoped application as TypeScript source on your own machine, using Fluent — a declarative library where each platform artifact (table, business rule, script include, ACL, REST API, flow, ATF test) is a typed function call. You then run a build that transforms that code into deployable metadata and pushes it to an instance.

The point is engineering discipline: your app lives in Git, so you get real diffs, pull requests, code review, and repeatable CI/CD builds — instead of shuttling Update Sets between instances.

import { BusinessRule } from '@servicenow/sdk/core'
import { setOrderPriority } from '../server/set-order-priority'

BusinessRule({
    $id: Now.ID['set_order_priority'],
    name: 'Set Order Priority',
    active: true,
    table: 'x_myapp_order',
    when: 'before',
    action: ['insert', 'update'],
    script: setOrderPriority, // preferred: JS module (Now.include still works)
})

The declarative "when it runs" lives in the .now.ts file; server logic preferably lives in a src/server module with typed Glide APIs. A project has now.config.json (scope + scopeId), src/fluent, and now-sdk build / now-sdk install steps.

SDK vs App Engine Studio

  • Choose the SDK/Fluent for engineering-led teams that want Git, code review, TypeScript types, and CI/CD across environments.
  • Choose App Engine Studio / the platform UI for fast low-code work by admins and citizen developers, or small single-instance apps.
  • They coexist — an SDK-built app still opens in the platform.
Score points: mention that Now.ID['...'] maps to stable sys_ids in src/fluent/generated/keys.ts (never hand-edit; never invent sys_ids), that JS modules are preferred over inlined Now.include scripts, that now-sdk install pushes the build to an instance, and that ServiceNow/sdk-examples plus now-sdk explain are the canonical references.

question: What is ServiceNow, and why do enterprises use it? Explain it as if you're talking to someone who has never heard of the platform.
answer:
Why Interviewers Ask This

This is the most common opening question in any ServiceNow interview. Interviewers want to see if you understand the 'why' behind the platform — not just the technical definition, but the business problem it solves.

The Answer

ServiceNow is a cloud-based platform that helps organizations manage their digital workflows. Think of it as a single system where an entire company can track, automate, and manage work — from IT support tickets to HR onboarding to security incidents to customer service requests.

Before ServiceNow, most companies had dozens of disconnected tools: one for IT tickets, another for change management, another for HR requests, another for asset tracking. Each team had their own spreadsheet, email inbox, or legacy tool. Nothing talked to each other. When an employee needed a laptop, they'd email IT, who'd email procurement, who'd email finance — all manually, with no visibility into where the request stood.

ServiceNow replaces that chaos with a single platform where:

  • Everything is a record on a table — incidents, changes, requests, assets, users — all stored in one connected database.
  • Workflows automate the boring stuff — approvals route automatically, notifications fire on schedule, escalations happen without someone remembering to follow up.
  • Everyone sees the same data — the employee sees their request status, the manager sees their team's workload, leadership sees dashboards and trends.

Why Enterprises Pay Millions for It

  • Scale: ServiceNow handles tens of thousands of users and millions of records. Fortune 500 companies run their entire IT operations on it.
  • Single platform: Instead of 20 tools with 20 vendors and 20 integration headaches, one platform handles IT Service Management (ITSM), IT Operations (ITOM), HR Service Delivery, Security Operations (SecOps), Customer Service (CSM), and more.
  • Out-of-the-box processes: ServiceNow comes with ITIL-aligned processes pre-built. Companies don't start from scratch — they configure and extend what's already there.
💡 Interview Tip

Don't just say 'it's a ticketing tool.' That's the fastest way to lose points. ServiceNow is a platform — ticketing is just one use case. Show that you understand it's an enterprise workflow engine that spans IT, HR, Security, and Customer Service.

question: What is ITSM, and what are the core ITIL processes that ServiceNow supports out of the box?
answer:
What This Question Really Tests

Almost every ServiceNow role touches ITSM (IT Service Management). Interviewers ask this to verify you understand the foundational processes — not just the tool, but the framework behind it.

The Answer

ITSM is a set of practices for managing IT services to meet business needs. ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) is the most widely adopted framework that defines these practices. ServiceNow implements ITIL processes as ready-to-use modules.

The Core ITIL Processes in ServiceNow

  • Incident Management: Something is broken right now. A user can't log in, a server is down, email isn't working. Goal: restore normal service as fast as possible. ServiceNow table: incident.
  • Problem Management: WHY did it break? After the fire is out, investigate the root cause so it doesn't happen again. A problem can be linked to multiple incidents. Table: problem.
  • Change Management: We want to make a change to the environment — deploy new code, patch a server, upgrade a network switch. Changes go through an approval and risk assessment process before implementation. Table: change_request.
  • Service Request Management: An employee needs something — a new laptop, software access, a VPN account. These are standard, pre-approved requests fulfilled through the Service Catalog. Table: sc_request / sc_req_item.
  • Knowledge Management: Documentation and self-service articles so users can solve common issues themselves. 'How do I reset my password?' → Knowledge Base article. Table: kb_knowledge.

How They Connect

// Real-world flow:
// 1. 50 users report 'email is slow' → 50 Incidents created
// 2. Service Desk links all 50 to one Problem → 'Exchange server memory leak'
// 3. Problem team identifies fix → Creates a Change Request
// 4. Change goes through CAB approval → Scheduled for Saturday night
// 5. Change implemented → Problem resolved → All 50 Incidents auto-closed
// 6. Knowledge article created: 'What to do if email is slow'
💡 Interview Tip

The classic follow-up is: 'What's the difference between an Incident and a Problem?' Incident = the symptom (something is broken NOW). Problem = the disease (WHY it keeps breaking). Nail this distinction and you'll stand out from 80% of candidates.

question: What are the different types of scripts in ServiceNow? List them, explain where each one runs, and give a one-line example of when you'd use each.
answer:
The Intent Behind This Question

This is a staple interview question because it tests whether you understand the client-server architecture. Many candidates mix up which scripts run where — and that's a red flag for interviewers.

Server-Side Scripts (run on the ServiceNow server)

  • Business Rules: Trigger automatically when a record is inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. Example: Auto-assign a P1 incident to the on-call team when it's created.
  • Script Includes: Reusable server-side JavaScript classes/functions. Called by Business Rules, other Script Includes, or from the client via GlideAjax. Example: A shared utility function that calculates SLA breach time, used by multiple Business Rules.
  • Scheduled Jobs (Scheduled Script Executions): Run on a defined schedule — daily, weekly, or at a specific time. Example: Every night at midnight, close all resolved incidents older than 7 days.
  • Fix Scripts: One-time scripts that run manually. Used for data cleanup or bulk updates. Example: Update all 5,000 legacy incidents to a new category structure after a migration.
  • Background Scripts: Ad-hoc scripts run by admins for testing or troubleshooting. Not saved or scheduled. Example: Quickly check how many open P1 incidents exist right now.

Client-Side Scripts (run in the user's browser)

  • Client Scripts: Trigger on form events — onLoad, onChange, onSubmit, onCellEdit. Example: When the 'Category' dropdown changes to 'Network', show the 'Network Device' field and make it mandatory.
  • UI Policies: Declarative (no-code) rules to make fields mandatory, read-only, or visible. Example: When Priority is 'Critical', make 'Assignment Group' mandatory — configured entirely through the UI, no code.
  • UI Actions: Custom buttons, links, or context menu items on forms or lists. Can run client-side, server-side, or both. Example: A 'Close and Notify' button that resolves the incident and sends the caller an email in one click.

The Golden Rule

// SERVER-SIDE: Has access to GlideRecord, can query/update database directly
// CLIENT-SIDE: Has access to g_form, g_user — manipulates the form in the browser
// 
// Client CANNOT use GlideRecord. To get server data from client, use GlideAjax.
// This is the #1 mistake beginners make.
💡 Interview Tip

If the interviewer asks 'Can you use GlideRecord in a Client Script?' — the answer is no. Client Scripts run in the browser; GlideRecord runs on the server. The bridge between them is GlideAjax. Getting this right shows you understand the architecture.

question: Explain the difference between an Incident, a Problem, a Change Request, and a Service Request. Give a real-world scenario that connects all four.
answer:
Why This Comes Up in Interviews

This question tests your ITIL fundamentals. Every ServiceNow admin and developer needs to know these four record types cold — they're the backbone of ITSM.

The Four Pillars

  • Incident: Something is broken or not working as expected RIGHT NOW. Focus: restore service as quickly as possible. Not about finding root cause — just get things working again. 'The printer on floor 3 isn't printing.'
  • Problem: The investigation into WHY incidents keep happening. Focus: find the root cause and eliminate it permanently. 'Floor 3 printer fails every Monday because the print spooler service crashes during the weekly backup.'
  • Change Request: A planned modification to the IT environment that goes through approval and risk assessment. Focus: minimize disruption while implementing necessary changes. 'Schedule a maintenance window to move the print spooler to a separate server so the backup doesn't crash it.'
  • Service Request: A standard, pre-approved request for something the user needs. No break/fix, no investigation, no risk assessment — just fulfillment. 'I need a new toner cartridge for the floor 3 printer.'

A Scenario That Connects All Four

// MONDAY 9:00 AM
// 15 employees report: 'I can't access the CRM application'
// → 15 Incidents created (INC0045001 through INC0045015)
// → Service Desk applies workaround: restart the app server
// → All 15 incidents resolved

// TUESDAY 9:00 AM
// Same thing happens again! 12 new incidents.
// → Service Desk creates a Problem (PRB0002001)
//   'CRM application crashes every morning around 9 AM'
// → Problem team investigates: the database connection pool
//   exhausts at peak login time because the pool size is too small

// WEDNESDAY
// → Problem team creates a Change Request (CHG0003001)
//   'Increase CRM database connection pool from 50 to 200'
// → Change goes to Change Advisory Board (CAB) for approval
// → Approved for Thursday night maintenance window

// THURSDAY NIGHT
// → Change implemented, tested, closed successful
// → Problem resolved, linked to Change
// → All related Incidents auto-updated

// MEANWHILE (unrelated)
// → Employee submits a Service Request: 'I need CRM admin access'
//   (RITM0006001) — goes through standard approval workflow

Key Relationships

  • Multiple Incidents can be linked to one Problem
  • A Problem can generate a Change Request as its fix
  • A Change Request resolves the Problem, which closes the Incidents
  • Service Requests are independent — they're about fulfilling needs, not fixing issues
💡 Interview Tip

Memorize this: Incident = firefighting. Problem = detective work. Change = planned surgery. Service Request = shopping. That analogy alone will make your answer memorable.

question: What is a Business Rule in ServiceNow? Explain the different types (before, after, async, display) and when each one fires.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Business Rules are the most important server-side automation in ServiceNow. Every developer and admin needs to know the four types and their execution timing.

What Is a Business Rule?

A Business Rule is a server-side script that runs automatically when a record is displayed, inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. Think of it as an automatic trigger — you define WHEN it fires and WHAT it does.

The Four Types

  • Before Business Rule: Fires BEFORE the record is saved to the database. Use it to validate data, modify field values, or abort the save entirely.
    // Example: Auto-set priority based on impact and urgency
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  if (current.impact == 1 && current.urgency == 1) {
    current.priority = 1; // Critical
  }
})(current, previous);
  • After Business Rule: Fires AFTER the record is successfully saved. The database write is complete. Use it for things that depend on the record existing — sending notifications, creating related records, updating other tables.
    // Example: Create a task when a change request is approved
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  if (current.approval.changesTo('approved')) { // Use internal value; 'approved' is the value for the approval field
    var task = new GlideRecord('change_task');
    task.initialize();
    task.change_request = current.sys_id;
    task.short_description = 'Implement: ' + current.short_description;
    task.insert();
  }
})(current, previous);
  • Async (Asynchronous) Business Rule: Fires AFTER the save but runs in the background on a separate thread. The user doesn't wait for it to finish. Use it for heavy operations — external API calls, complex calculations, bulk updates.
    // Example: Sync incident data to an external monitoring system
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('MonitoringSystem', 'POST');
  rm.setStringParameterNoEscape('incident_id', current.number);
  rm.execute(); // Runs in background — user doesn't wait
})(current, previous);
  • Display Business Rule: Fires when a form is loaded (displayed) to the user. Does NOT run on list views, imports, or web service calls. Use it to calculate display-only values or pass data to client scripts via the g_scratchpad object.
    // Example: Show a warning message when a VIP's incident is opened
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  if (current.caller_id.vip == true) {
    g_scratchpad.isVIP = true; // Pass to client script
  }
})(current, previous);

Execution Order

// When a user clicks 'Save' on an incident form:
// 1. Client Script (onSubmit) — browser validates
// 2. Data sent to server
// 3. BEFORE Business Rules — server validates/modifies
// 4. DATABASE WRITE — record saved
// 5. AFTER Business Rules — post-save logic
// 6. ASYNC Business Rules — queued for background execution
//
// When a user OPENS a form:
// 1. Database read
// 2. DISPLAY Business Rules — prepare display data
// 3. Form renders in browser
// 4. Client Script (onLoad) — browser-side setup
💡 Interview Tip

The follow-up question is always: 'Can you access the previous object in an async Business Rule?' The answer is no — async BRs don't have access to the previous values because they run outside the original transaction. If you need to compare old vs new values, do it in a before/after BR and store the result.

question: What is a sys_id in ServiceNow? Why is it important, and where will you encounter it?
answer:
Reading Between the Lines

This seems like a basic question, but it reveals whether you understand ServiceNow's data model at a fundamental level. sys_id is everywhere in ServiceNow, and misunderstanding it causes real bugs.

The Answer

A sys_id is a 32-character globally unique identifier (GUID) automatically assigned to every record in every table in ServiceNow. It's the primary key — the one field that uniquely identifies a record across the entire instance.

// Example sys_id:
// 6816f79cc0a8016401c5a33be04be441
//
// Every record has one:
// Incident INC0010001 → sys_id: 5137153cc611227c000bbd1bd8cd2005
// User 'John Smith'  → sys_id: 6816f79cc0a8016401c5a33be04be441
// Business Rule 'Set Priority' → sys_id: a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6

Why It Matters

  • Reference fields use sys_id: When an incident has a 'Caller' field pointing to John Smith, the database stores John's sys_id (not his name). The display name is resolved at render time.
  • APIs use sys_id: REST API calls reference records by sys_id. GET /api/now/table/incident/5137153cc611227c000bbd1bd8cd2005
  • Scripts use sys_id: gr.get('5137153cc611227c000bbd1bd8cd2005') fetches a specific record. gr.getValue('caller_id') returns a sys_id, not a name.
  • URLs contain sys_id: When you open an incident form, the URL includes sys_id=5137153cc611227c000bbd1bd8cd2005.

Common Mistakes

// MISTAKE 1: Comparing display value instead of sys_id
if (current.caller_id == 'John Smith')  // WRONG — comparing GlideElement to string
if (current.getValue('caller_id') == '6816f79cc0a8016401c5a33be04be441')  // CORRECT

// MISTAKE 2: Hardcoding sys_ids across instances
// sys_ids are PRESERVED during instance cloning.
// However, records created independently on separate instances
// (e.g., a Business Rule built by hand in dev and separately in prod)
// will have different sys_ids.
// Never hardcode sys_ids — use queries or system properties instead.

// CORRECT approach: Query by a stable identifier
var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
gr.addQuery('user_name', 'john.smith');  // Stable across instances
gr.query();
if (gr.next()) {
  var userId = gr.sys_id; // Now use this dynamically
}
💡 Interview Tip

If asked 'What does getValue() return for a reference field?' — always say the sys_id. If you want the display name, use getDisplayValue(). This distinction comes up in almost every technical ServiceNow interview.

question: What is the difference between a Client Script and a UI Policy? When would you choose one over the other?
answer:
The Real Question

Both Client Scripts and UI Policies run on the client side (in the browser) and both manipulate the form. The confusion is real — interviewers want to hear you explain the clear boundary between declarative and scripted approaches.

UI Policy (No-Code / Declarative)

A UI Policy uses conditions configured through the UI to control field behavior — no code required.

  • What it can do: Make a field mandatory, make it read-only, show/hide a field.
  • How it works: You set a condition (e.g., 'Priority is Critical') and define actions (e.g., 'Set Assignment Group to Mandatory'). All configured via dropdowns — no JavaScript.
  • Best for: Simple, condition-based field behaviors that admins (non-developers) can manage.

Client Script (Code / Imperative)

A Client Script uses JavaScript to react to form events — much more flexible but requires coding knowledge.

  • Types: onLoad (form opens), onChange (field value changes), onSubmit (form is submitted), onCellEdit (list editing).
  • What it can do: Everything a UI Policy does, PLUS: show alerts, make API calls (GlideAjax), set field values dynamically, perform complex calculations, interact with multiple fields at once.
// UI Policy equivalent in Client Script:
// 'When Priority is Critical, make Assignment Group mandatory'
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
  if (isLoading) return;
  if (newValue == '1') { // Priority = Critical
    g_form.setMandatory('assignment_group', true);
  } else {
    g_form.setMandatory('assignment_group', false);
  }
}

Decision Guide

  • Need to make a field mandatory/read-only/visible based on a simple condition? → UI Policy
  • Need to set a field's value based on another field? → Client Script (onChange)
  • Need to call the server for data? → Client Script + GlideAjax
  • Need to validate before the form saves? → Client Script (onSubmit)
  • Need non-developers to maintain the rule? → UI Policy

Important Gotcha

If both a UI Policy and a Client Script control the same field, the UI Policy wins because it runs after the Client Script. This is a common source of bugs — one developer sets a field with a Client Script, another admin creates a UI Policy that overrides it, and neither understands why their change 'doesn't work.'

💡 Interview Tip

The safe answer is: 'Use UI Policy for simple field visibility/mandatory/read-only rules. Use Client Script for anything that requires logic, calculations, or server calls. And never use both on the same field — it creates conflicts.'

question: What are Update Sets in ServiceNow? How do you move customizations from a development instance to production?
answer:
Context

Every ServiceNow environment has separate instances (dev, test, prod). Update Sets are how you package and move your changes between them. This is the deployment mechanism — and understanding it is essential for any role.

What Is an Update Set?

An Update Set is a container that automatically captures every configuration change you make while it's active. When you modify a Business Rule, create a UI Policy, or add a field to a table — that change is recorded in your current Update Set.

The Migration Process

// Step-by-step deployment:
//
// 1. SET your Update Set (Dev instance)
//    System Settings → Developer tab → Select 'My Feature Update Set'
//    Everything you change is now captured here
//
// 2. MAKE your changes
//    Create Business Rules, modify forms, add fields, etc.
//    Each change = one record in the Update Set
//
// 3. COMPLETE the Update Set
//    Mark it as 'Complete' — no more changes can be added
//
// 4. EXPORT from Dev
//    Right-click → Export to XML (or use Remote instance connection)
//
// 5. IMPORT to Test/Prod
//    Retrieved Update Sets → Import from XML
//
// 6. PREVIEW
//    System previews all changes and flags conflicts
//    'This Business Rule already exists — overwrite?'
//
// 7. COMMIT
//    Apply all changes to the target instance

What Update Sets Capture (and Don't)

  • DO capture: Business Rules, Client Scripts, UI Policies, UI Actions, Script Includes, ACLs, form layouts, System Properties, Scheduled Jobs, Flow Designer flows, table schema changes (new fields/tables).
  • DON'T capture: Data records (incidents, users, CMDB CIs), homepage/dashboard configurations (user-specific), report definitions (sometimes), attachment content.

Common Mistakes

  • Wrong Update Set: Forgetting to switch your active Update Set before making changes. Your changes end up in the 'Default' Update Set and get mixed with other unrelated work. Always check your current Update Set before starting.
  • Missing dependencies: You create a Script Include in one Update Set and a Business Rule that calls it in another. If you deploy the Business Rule first, it fails because the Script Include doesn't exist yet. Always track dependencies and deploy in order.
  • Overwriting changes: Two developers modify the same Business Rule in different Update Sets. The second one committed overwrites the first — no merge, just overwrite. Communication is critical.
💡 Interview Tip

If asked 'How is this different from Git?' — explain that Update Sets capture configuration changes automatically (you don't 'commit' individual changes), there's no branching or merging, and the last commit wins on conflicts. For scoped applications, ServiceNow now offers Source Control Integration with Git, which is closer to what modern developers expect.

question: What is an ACL (Access Control List) in ServiceNow? How does it protect data?
answer:
Why This Matters in an Interview

Security is a core topic in every ServiceNow interview. ACLs control who can read, write, create, and delete data — and they're enforced automatically across the entire platform.

What Is an ACL?

An ACL is a security rule that controls access to tables, records, and individual fields. When a user tries to view an incident, update a change request, or delete a CI — the platform checks the ACLs to determine if that action is allowed.

The Three Components of an ACL

  • 1. Roles: Which role(s) does the user need? e.g., itil, admin, incident_manager. A user must have the specified role to pass this check.
  • 2. Conditions: Filter conditions on the record. e.g., 'Only if the record is assigned to the user's group.' This provides row-level security.
  • 3. Script: Advanced JavaScript logic for complex authorization. Returns true (allow) or false (deny).
// ACL Example:
// Table: incident
// Operation: write
// Role required: itil
// Condition: active=true
// Meaning: Users with 'itil' role can edit incidents, but only active ones

// ACL Script Example:
// Allow editing only if the incident belongs to the user's assignment group
answer = gs.getUser().isMemberOf(current.assignment_group);

Evaluation Order

  • ACLs are matched from most specific to least specific — the first match at each level is the one that gets evaluated:
  • incident.caller_id — field-level ACL (most specific)
  • incident.* — table-level ACL
  • *.* — global ACL (least specific)
  • To reach a field, the user must pass both the matching field-level ACL and the matching table-level ACL. But when several ACLs match at the same point (e.g., two ACLs on incident.caller_id), passing any one of them grants access (OR) — so adding another ACL at the same level can actually loosen access.

Key Facts for Interviews

  • Deny by default: If no ACL grants access, access is denied. Unlike some systems where everything is open unless restricted.
  • Admin bypasses ACLs: Users with the admin role skip ACL checks entirely (unless the ACL script explicitly handles admin).
  • Applies everywhere: ACLs enforce on UI, REST API, list views, reports, exports — not just forms.
💡 Interview Tip

The classic trick question: 'If I create a read ACL on the incident table requiring the itil role, and another read ACL on incident.priority requiring the incident_manager role — what happens when a user with only the itil role opens an incident?' Answer: They can see the incident (table ACL passes) but the priority field will be hidden/empty (field ACL fails). Both ACLs evaluate independently.

question: What is GlideRecord? Write a basic GlideRecord query to find all open P1 incidents assigned to a specific group.
answer:
Setting the Stage

GlideRecord is the single most important API in ServiceNow development. If there's one thing you need to know for any technical interview, it's this. Every developer, admin, and consultant uses GlideRecord daily.

What Is GlideRecord?

GlideRecord is a server-side JavaScript API that lets you query, insert, update, and delete records from any ServiceNow table. It's your primary tool for interacting with the database — like SQL queries, but in JavaScript.

Basic Operations

// === QUERY (SELECT) ===
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');     // Target the incident table
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);               // WHERE priority = 1
gr.addQuery('state', '!=', 6);            // AND state != Resolved
gr.addQuery('assignment_group.name', 'Network Support'); // AND group name
gr.orderByDesc('sys_created_on');         // ORDER BY created descending
gr.setLimit(50);                          // LIMIT 50
gr.query();                               // Execute the query

while (gr.next()) {                       // Iterate through results
  gs.info('Incident: ' + gr.getValue('number'));
  gs.info('Caller: ' + gr.getDisplayValue('caller_id'));
  gs.info('Created: ' + gr.getValue('sys_created_on'));
}

// === INSERT ===
var newInc = new GlideRecord('incident');
newInc.initialize();
newInc.short_description = 'Server Down - Building A';
newInc.priority = 1;
// Look up the caller by user_name to get their sys_id
var caller = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
caller.addQuery('user_name', 'john.smith');
caller.query();
if (caller.next()) {
  newInc.caller_id = caller.sys_id;
}
var newSysId = newInc.insert();  // Returns the sys_id of new record

// === UPDATE ===
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');   // Get a specific incident
gr.state = 6;                     // Set state to Resolved
gr.close_notes = 'Fixed by restarting the service';
gr.update();                      // Save changes

// === DELETE ===
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');
gr.deleteRecord();                // Delete the record

Key Methods to Know

  • addQuery(field, value) — adds a WHERE condition
  • addQuery(field, operator, value) — adds a WHERE with operator (!=, >, <, IN, etc.)
  • addEncodedQuery(string) — adds a complex filter as encoded query string
  • query() — executes the query
  • next() — moves to the next record (returns false when done)
  • getValue(field) — returns the raw database value
  • getDisplayValue(field) — returns the display value
  • getRowCount() — executes a full COUNT(*) query; avoid on large tables. Use GlideAggregate with addAggregate('COUNT') instead
  • get(field, value) — shortcut to query a single record
💡 Interview Tip

When writing GlideRecord in an interview, always include setLimit() for queries on large tables, always use getValue() instead of dot-notation for field values, and always add if (isLoading) return; at the top if it's inside a Client Script. These small details signal experience.

question: What is the Service Catalog in ServiceNow? How is it different from the regular incident form, and what happens when a user submits a catalog request?
answer:
Why Interviewers Ask This

The Service Catalog is one of the most visible parts of ServiceNow for end users. Interviewers want to see that you understand the full request lifecycle — not just the front-end form.

What Is the Service Catalog?

The Service Catalog is a self-service portal where employees can browse and request services or products — like an internal shopping site. Instead of sending emails or calling the help desk, users find what they need, fill out a form, and submit.

Catalog vs Incident — The Key Difference

  • Incident: Something is BROKEN. Reactive. 'My laptop won't turn on.' The goal is to fix it fast.
  • Service Request (Catalog): The user WANTS something. Proactive. 'I need a new laptop.' The goal is to fulfill the order through a defined process.

The Components

  • Catalog Item: A requestable service or product. 'Request a Laptop', 'VPN Access', 'New Hire Onboarding Package'.
  • Variables: The form fields specific to that item. Laptop model dropdown, justification text field, delivery date picker.
  • Variable Sets: Reusable groups of variables shared across multiple catalog items. A 'Delivery Address' variable set used by laptop, monitor, and phone requests.
  • Workflow / Flow: The backend process that handles approval and fulfillment.

What Happens When a User Submits

// User clicks 'Order Now' on 'Request a Laptop'
//
// 1. REQUEST created (sc_request) — REQ0010001
//    The overall 'order' record
//
// 2. REQUESTED ITEM created (sc_req_item) — RITM0010001
//    The specific line item (one per catalog item ordered)
//    Contains all the variable values (laptop model, etc.)
//
// 3. APPROVAL triggered
//    Flow/Workflow checks: Does this need manager approval?
//    If cost > $500, route to manager → If approved, continue
//
// 4. CATALOG TASKS created (sc_task)
//    SCTASK0010001: 'Procurement: Order laptop from vendor'
//    SCTASK0010002: 'IT: Configure laptop and install software'
//    SCTASK0010003: 'Facilities: Ship to employee's desk'
//
// 5. Each task assigned to the relevant team
//    Teams work their tasks independently
//
// 6. All tasks complete → RITM auto-closes → REQ auto-closes
//    User gets a notification: 'Your laptop is on its way!'
💡 Interview Tip

Know the table relationships: sc_request (the order) → sc_req_item (the line item) → sc_task (the fulfillment tasks). If asked 'Where are the user's variable answers stored?' — values are stored in the sc_item_option table, linked to the RITM via the sc_item_option_mtom many-to-many table.

question: What is a GlideAjax call, and why do you need it? Write a simple example of a Client Script calling a server-side Script Include using GlideAjax.
answer:
What This Question Really Tests

This is a top-tier beginner question because it tests understanding of the client-server boundary — the most important architectural concept in ServiceNow development.

Why You Need GlideAjax

Client Scripts run in the browser. They can manipulate the form with g_form, but they cannot query the database directly. GlideRecord is a server-side-only API. So when a Client Script needs data from the database, it must ask the server — and GlideAjax is the mechanism for that request.

Think of it as making an AJAX call to a backend API endpoint, except the 'endpoint' is a Script Include method.

Step-by-Step Example

// ============================================
// STEP 1: Create the Script Include (server-side)
// Name: UserInfoHelper
// Accessible from: All application scopes
// ============================================
var UserInfoHelper = Class.create();
UserInfoHelper.prototype = Object.extendsObject(
  AbstractAjaxProcessor, {  // MUST extend this for GlideAjax
  
  // This method will be callable from the client
  getUserDepartment: function() {
    var userId = this.getParameter('sysparm_user_id');
    var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
    if (gr.get(userId)) {
      return gr.getDisplayValue('department');
    }
    return 'Unknown';
  },
  
  type: 'UserInfoHelper'
});

// ============================================
// STEP 2: Create the Client Script (client-side)
// Type: onChange
// Field: caller_id
// ============================================
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
  if (isLoading || newValue === '') return;
  
  // Create the GlideAjax call
  var ga = new GlideAjax('UserInfoHelper');  // Script Include name
  ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getUserDepartment'); // Method to call
  ga.addParam('sysparm_user_id', newValue);  // Pass the user's sys_id
  
  // Make the call (asynchronous — doesn't freeze the form)
  ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
    // 'answer' contains the return value from the server
    g_form.setValue('u_department', answer);
  });
}

How It Works

  • Client Script creates a GlideAjax object pointing to the Script Include name
  • Passes the method name via sysparm_name parameter
  • Passes any custom data via additional sysparm_ parameters
  • Calls getXMLAnswer() with a callback function — this is asynchronous
  • ServiceNow server receives the request, instantiates the Script Include, calls the method, and returns the result
  • The callback function receives the result and updates the form

Important Rules

  • The Script Include must extend AbstractAjaxProcessor to be callable via GlideAjax
  • Use this.getParameter('sysparm_xxx') to read parameters on the server side
  • Always use the asynchronous pattern (getXMLAnswer) — the synchronous version (getXMLWait) freezes the browser
  • Return values are always strings — if you need objects, use JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse()
💡 Interview Tip

If asked to whiteboard a GlideAjax call, always include: (1) the Script Include extending AbstractAjaxProcessor, (2) the Client Script with sysparm_name, and (3) the asynchronous callback. Missing any of these three pieces signals you've only read about it, not used it.

question: What are the different tables in ServiceNow, and what does 'table extends table' mean? Give an example.
answer:
The Intent Behind This Question

Table inheritance is one of ServiceNow's most important concepts. It affects how data is stored, how scripts execute, and how security is applied. Interviewers ask this to check if you understand why a Business Rule on 'task' fires on incidents too.

Tables in ServiceNow

Every piece of data in ServiceNow lives in a table. Tables are like database tables — they have columns (fields) and rows (records). But ServiceNow tables support inheritance, which means one table can extend another and inherit all its fields.

The Task Table Hierarchy

// task (base table)
// ├── Fields: number, state, priority, assigned_to, short_description
// │
// ├── incident (extends task)
// │   └── Adds: category, subcategory, caller_id, resolve_time
// │
// ├── change_request (extends task)
// │   └── Adds: risk, type, planned_start_date, cab_required
// │
// ├── problem (extends task)
// │   └── Adds: known_error, root_cause, workaround
// │
// ├── sc_task (extends task)
// │   └── Adds: request_item, catalog fields
// │
// └── sc_req_item (extends task)
//     └── Adds: cat_item, stage, price
//     NOTE: sc_req_item extends task directly, NOT sc_task

What 'Extends' Means in Practice

  • Field inheritance: The incident table has all fields from task (number, state, priority...) PLUS its own fields (category, caller_id). You don't need to recreate common fields.
  • Script inheritance: A Business Rule on the task table fires for ALL child tables — incidents, changes, problems, etc. This is powerful but dangerous if unintended.
  • ACL inheritance: A security rule on task applies to all extending tables unless overridden at the child level.
  • Physical storage: ServiceNow uses single-table inheritance — child records are physically stored in the parent table's database. A sys_class_name field acts as a discriminator to identify the record type.
// Important: Querying 'task' returns EVERYTHING
var gr = new GlideRecord('task');
gr.addQuery('assigned_to', userId);
gr.query();
// Returns incidents + changes + problems + catalog tasks + ...
// Could be hundreds of thousands of records!

// If you only want incidents, query the child table:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('assigned_to', userId);
gr.query();
// Returns only incidents

Other Important Tables (Non-Task)

  • sys_user — User records
  • sys_user_group — Group records
  • cmdb_ci — Configuration Items (extends to cmdb_ci_server, cmdb_ci_database, etc.)
  • kb_knowledge — Knowledge articles
  • sys_choice — Dropdown/choice list values
💡 Interview Tip

Always check if the table you're working with extends another table before writing a Business Rule. The classic mistake: writing a BR on 'task' thinking it only affects your custom task type, then discovering it fires on every incident, change, and problem in the system.

question: What is the difference between getValue() and getDisplayValue() in GlideRecord? Why does this matter?
answer:
Why This Comes Up in Interviews

This is one of the most frequently asked questions in ServiceNow interviews at all levels. It tests whether you understand how ServiceNow stores data vs how it displays data — a critical distinction that causes real bugs.

The Core Difference

  • getValue() — Returns the raw value stored in the database (internal value)
  • getDisplayValue() — Returns the human-readable value shown to users

Where They Differ

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');

// REFERENCE FIELDS (biggest difference)
gr.getValue('caller_id');         // '6816f79cc0a8016401c5a33be04be441' (sys_id)
gr.getDisplayValue('caller_id');  // 'John Smith' (display name)

// CHOICE FIELDS
gr.getValue('state');             // '1' (internal number)
gr.getDisplayValue('state');      // 'New' (label text)

gr.getValue('priority');          // '1' (internal number)
gr.getDisplayValue('priority');   // '1 - Critical' (label text)

// DATE/TIME FIELDS
gr.getValue('opened_at');         // '2026-03-15 14:30:00' (UTC, internal)
gr.getDisplayValue('opened_at');  // '2026-03-15 09:30:00' (user's timezone)

// STRING FIELDS (no difference)
gr.getValue('short_description');        // 'Server is down'
gr.getDisplayValue('short_description'); // 'Server is down'

Why It Matters

  • For comparisons, always use getValue():
    // WRONG — display values can change with language settings
if (gr.getDisplayValue('state') == 'New') { ... }

// CORRECT — internal values are consistent
if (gr.getValue('state') == '1') { ... }
  • For displaying to users, use getDisplayValue():
    // For messages, emails, notifications:
gs.info('Assigned to: ' + gr.getDisplayValue('assigned_to'));
// Shows: 'Assigned to: Jane Doe' (not a sys_id)
  • For integrations, use getValue():
    // External systems need consistent, language-independent values
var payload = {
  state: gr.getValue('state'),           // '1' — always the same
  assignee: gr.getValue('assigned_to')   // sys_id — stable reference
};
💡 Interview Tip

The follow-up trap: 'What does gr.caller_id return without using getValue or getDisplayValue?' Answer: it returns a GlideElement object — not a string. This object behaves unpredictably in comparisons. Always use getValue() or getDisplayValue() explicitly to avoid subtle bugs.

question: What is the Import Set and Transform Map in ServiceNow? Describe a scenario where you'd use them.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Data import is a critical operation in every ServiceNow implementation. Import Sets and Transform Maps are how external data (CSV files, API feeds, Excel spreadsheets) gets loaded into ServiceNow tables.

The Two-Step Process

  • Import Set: The raw data landing zone. External data is loaded into a temporary staging table first — not directly into the target table. This staging table is called an Import Set table.
  • Transform Map: The mapping rules that convert staging data into target table records. It defines which source column maps to which target field, and includes logic for data transformation and upsert handling.

Real Scenario: Employee Onboarding

// HR sends a CSV every Monday with new hires:
// first_name, last_name, email, department, start_date
// John, Smith, john.smith@company.com, Engineering, 2026-04-01
// Jane, Doe, jane.doe@company.com, Marketing, 2026-04-01

// STEP 1: Data Source (scheduled or manual)
// Configure a Data Source pointing to the CSV file location
// ServiceNow reads the CSV and loads rows into staging table

// STEP 2: Import Set (staging table)
// Table: u_new_hire_import
// Each CSV row becomes a record in this staging table
// Data is raw — no validation yet

// STEP 3: Transform Map
// Maps staging columns to target table (sys_user):
//   u_first_name  → first_name
//   u_last_name   → last_name  
//   u_email       → email
//   u_department  → department (lookup by name)
//   u_start_date  → u_start_date
//
// Coalesce field: email
// If email exists in sys_user → UPDATE that record
// If email doesn't exist → INSERT new record

// STEP 4: Transform runs
// Each staging row is transformed and written to sys_user
// Transform scripts can run additional logic:
(function transformRow(source, target, map, log, action) {
  // Auto-generate user_name from email
  target.user_name = source.u_email.toString().split('@')[0];
  // Set default password
  target.user_password = 'Welcome2026!';
})(source, target, map, log, action);

Key Concepts

  • Coalesce field: The matching key for upsert logic. If a record with this value exists in the target, UPDATE it. If not, INSERT a new one.
  • Transform scripts: Run before/after each row or at the start/end of the entire import. Use for data cleanup, validation, or custom logic.
  • Import Set Run: Each import execution creates a 'run' record with success/failure counts. Check here for errors.
💡 Interview Tip

The typical gotcha question: 'What happens if you set the wrong coalesce field?' If the field isn't unique (e.g., 'department' instead of 'email'), the transform will update the FIRST matching record for all rows with the same department — destroying data. Always choose a unique identifier as the coalesce field.

question: What are Roles and Groups in ServiceNow? How do they work together to control what users can see and do?
answer:
Reading Between the Lines

Every ServiceNow interview touches on user management. Roles and Groups are the foundation of security and task routing — understanding how they connect is essential.

Roles vs Groups

  • Role: Defines WHAT a user can do. A role grants permissions — access to modules, ability to read/write tables, visibility of UI elements. Examples: itil (IT staff), admin (full access), incident_manager, catalog_admin.
  • Group: Defines WHO works together. A group is a collection of users — typically a team. Examples: 'Network Support', 'Database Admins', 'HR Service Desk'. Groups are used for task assignment and routing.

How They Connect

// A user can have:
// - Roles assigned directly (user → role)
// - Roles inherited through groups (user → group → role)
//
// Example:
// User: Jane Doe
//   └── Group: 'Network Support' team
//         └── Group has role: 'itil'
//         └── Group has role: 'network_admin'
//   └── Direct role: 'change_manager'
//
// Result: Jane has itil + network_admin (from group) + change_manager (direct)

// Groups are also used for ASSIGNMENT:
// When a P1 Network incident comes in:
// → Assignment Group = 'Network Support'
// → Any member of that group can pick it up
// → The group manager gets escalation notifications

Common Role Types

  • admin — Full system access. Bypasses all ACLs. Use sparingly.
  • itil — Standard IT staff role. Access to incident, problem, change modules.
  • catalog_admin — Manage Service Catalog items and categories.
  • knowledge_admin — Manage Knowledge Base articles.
  • approver_user — Can approve/reject requests and changes.

Important Distinctions

  • Roles control access: Can this user SEE the incident table? Can they EDIT change requests? Can they DELETE records?
  • Groups control routing: Which TEAM should this ticket go to? Who gets notified? Who's in the approval chain?
  • A user without a group can still have roles and access. They just won't receive group-assigned work.
  • A user in a group inherits the group's roles automatically.
💡 Interview Tip

If asked 'How would you give a new IT support agent access to manage incidents?' — don't say 'give them admin.' Say: 'Add them to the appropriate support group, which should already have the itil role. They'll inherit the role from the group and be able to see incidents assigned to their team.' This shows you understand the proper model.

question: What is Flow Designer in ServiceNow? How is it different from a Workflow, and when would you use each?
answer:
The Real Question

ServiceNow has two automation engines — the legacy Workflow Editor and the modern Flow Designer. Interviewers ask this to see if you know the platform's direction and can make the right choice for new projects.

Flow Designer (Modern — Recommended)

  • Low-code, drag-and-drop automation builder
  • Trigger: record created/updated, scheduled, inbound email, REST call, or custom
  • Actions: create/update records, send notifications, make REST calls, approvals, subflows
  • Supports error handling (try/catch), parallel execution, and loops
  • Can call Integration Hub spokes (pre-built connectors for Slack, Teams, Jira, etc.)
  • ServiceNow's strategic direction — all new features ship here first

Workflow Editor (Legacy — Still Supported)

  • Older drag-and-drop engine with a more visual canvas
  • Graphical state-machine approach — boxes and arrows
  • Well-established, millions of existing workflows in production
  • No longer receiving new features or significant investment
  • Still works, still supported, but new projects should use Flow Designer

A Simple Flow Example

// Flow: Auto-Escalate Unassigned P1 Incidents
//
// TRIGGER: Record Updated → incident table
//   Condition: Priority = 1 AND Assignment Group is empty
//              AND State = New AND Created > 15 minutes ago
//
// ACTION 1: Look Up Record
//   Table: sys_user_group
//   Condition: name = 'Critical Incident Team'
//
// ACTION 2: Update Record
//   Target: Trigger → Incident Record
//   Set Assignment Group = Step 1 result
//   Set Comments = 'Auto-escalated: P1 unassigned for 15+ min'
//
// ACTION 3: Send Notification
//   To: Critical Incident Team members
//   Subject: 'P1 Escalation: ' + Incident Number
//
// No code needed. All configured through the Flow Designer UI.

When to Use Each

  • New project? → Flow Designer. Always.
  • Maintaining existing workflow? → Keep it in Workflow Editor unless you have a reason to migrate.
  • Complex multi-system integration? → Flow Designer + Integration Hub spokes.
  • Need reusable automation? → Build a Subflow in Flow Designer — callable from other flows (like a function).
💡 Interview Tip

Never say 'I'd use the Workflow Editor for a new project.' That signals outdated knowledge. The safe answer: 'Flow Designer for anything new. Workflow Editor only if we're maintaining legacy automations that haven't been migrated yet.' If asked about Process Automation Designer (PAD), mention it's for complex multi-stage processes that orchestrate multiple flows — like an end-to-end employee onboarding journey.

question: What are Notifications in ServiceNow? How do you configure an email notification that fires when a P1 incident is created?
answer:
Context

Notifications are one of the first things configured in any ITSM implementation. Every interviewer expects you to know how they work — from basic configuration to when scripts are needed.

How Notifications Work

ServiceNow Notifications are email (or SMS/push) alerts triggered by record events. They have three parts: WHO gets it, WHEN it fires, and WHAT it says.

Configuring a P1 Incident Notification

// Notification Configuration:
//
// NAME: 'P1 Incident Created Alert'
// TABLE: incident
//
// WHEN TO SEND:
//   Send when: Record inserted
//   Conditions: Priority = 1 - Critical
//   (Optional advanced condition script for complex logic)
//
// WHO RECEIVES:
//   Users: (specific users, e.g., IT Director)
//   Groups: 'Critical Incident Team'
//   Users in fields: Assignment Group Manager
//   Events: Can also trigger via Event Registry
//
// WHAT IT SAYS:
//   Subject: 'P1 CRITICAL: ${number} - ${short_description}'
//   Body (HTML):
//   'A Critical incident has been created.
//    Number: ${number}
//    Description: ${short_description}
//    Caller: ${caller_id.name}
//    Created: ${sys_created_on}
//    Link: ${URI_REF}'
//
// ${field_name} = mail script variable — replaced with actual values

Three Ways to Trigger Notifications

  • Direct conditions: When a record matches specific conditions on insert/update. Simplest approach — configured entirely through the UI.
  • Event-driven: A Business Rule fires an event → the event triggers the notification. More flexible — decouples the trigger logic from the notification. Better for complex scenarios.
    // Business Rule fires the event:
gs.eventQueue('incident.priority.critical', current, 
  current.assigned_to, current.assignment_group);

// Notification listens for the event:
// Event name: incident.priority.critical
  • Flow Designer: A flow action sends the notification as part of an automated workflow. Best for multi-step processes.

Key Configuration Points

  • Weight: Each notification has a numeric weight. When multiple notifications for the same record and recipients would send, only the highest-weight one is delivered — the rest are skipped. The default weight 0 means the notification always sends. Use weights to prevent duplicate emails.
  • Digest: Batch multiple notifications into a single daily/hourly email instead of spamming users.
  • Subscribe: Users can subscribe/unsubscribe from certain notification types.
💡 Interview Tip

If asked 'What's the best practice: direct notification or event-driven?' — the answer is event-driven for production. Direct notifications are fine for simple cases, but events give you flexibility to change what happens (email, Slack, SMS) without modifying the Business Rule. It follows the principle of loose coupling.

question: You've spent 12 years building .NET applications with Entity Framework. Your new team tells you ServiceNow uses 'GlideRecord' to interact with data. Walk me through how GlideRecord compares to what you already know — DbContext, LINQ queries, and EF migrations. What would surprise you the most coming from that world?
answer:
Why This Matters in an Interview

This question tests whether a seasoned .NET developer can mentally map their existing ORM knowledge to ServiceNow's server-side data API. Interviewers want to see that you're not starting from zero — you're translating.

The Direct Mapping

GlideRecord is ServiceNow's server-side API for database operations. If Entity Framework is your ORM that abstracts SQL into C# objects, GlideRecord is the equivalent abstraction layer — but with key differences:

// .NET Entity Framework (what you know)
var incidents = dbContext.Incidents
  .Where(i => i.Priority == 1 && i.State == "New")
  .OrderByDescending(i => i.CreatedOn)
  .Take(10)
  .ToList();

// ServiceNow GlideRecord (the equivalent)
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.addQuery('state', 'New');
gr.orderByDesc('sys_created_on');
gr.setLimit(10);
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  // Each gr.next() moves the cursor — like a DataReader
  gs.info(gr.getValue('number'));
}

What Surprises .NET Developers

  • No model classes: There's no Incident.cs with typed properties. GlideRecord fields are accessed by string name — gr.getValue('priority') not incident.Priority. It feels like working with DataRow instead of strongly-typed entities.
  • Cursor-based, not collection-based: GlideRecord behaves like SqlDataReader, not List<T>. You iterate with while(gr.next()), not foreach. There's no .ToList() that materializes everything into memory.
  • No migrations: Schema changes happen through the UI or Update Sets — not code-first migrations. Adding a column to a table is a point-and-click operation, not an Add-Migration command.
  • getValue() vs dot-walking: gr.caller_id returns a GlideElement object (not the value). Use gr.getValue('caller_id') for the raw sys_id or gr.getDisplayValue('caller_id') for the display name — similar to how EF navigation properties vs foreign key IDs work.
💡 .NET Developer Pro Tip

Think of GlideRecord as ADO.NET's DataReader wrapped with a query builder. It's not as elegant as LINQ, but the mental model is identical: build a query, execute it, iterate results. Your instincts about N+1 queries, limiting result sets, and indexing all transfer directly.

question: In your .NET projects, you've used middleware, action filters, and database triggers to intercept requests at different points. ServiceNow has something called 'Business Rules' that run on database operations. If an interviewer asks you — 'When does a Business Rule fire, and how is it different from what you've built in ASP.NET middleware?' — what's your answer?
answer:
Setting the Stage

Business Rules are server-side scripts that execute when a record is inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. They are the closest equivalent to a combination of ASP.NET middleware, Entity Framework interceptors, and SQL triggers — depending on the type.

The Execution Pipeline

// ASP.NET Request Pipeline (what you know)
// Request → Middleware → Controller → Action Filter → DB → Response
//
// ServiceNow Record Pipeline (the equivalent)
// Form Submit → Client Script (onSubmit) →
//   → Business Rule (before) → DATABASE WRITE →
//   → Business Rule (after) →
//   → Business Rule (async) [queued, runs later]
//   → Display Business Rule (on form load only)

Mapping to .NET Concepts

  • Before Business Rule = ActionExecutingContext in an Action Filter, or an EF SaveChanges interceptor. Runs before the database write. You can modify the record, validate, or abort. Like calling context.Result = new BadRequestResult() to short-circuit.
  • After Business Rule = Post-action filter or an AfterSaveChanges hook. The record is already saved. Use for cascade updates, notifications, or audit logging — things you'd do in a DbContext.SavedChanges event.
  • Async Business Rule = A message queued to a background worker, like publishing to an Azure Service Bus or Hangfire job. The user's transaction completes immediately; processing happens later on ServiceNow's scheduler.
  • Display Business Rule = Like a ViewComponent or OnGet() handler in Razor Pages. Runs when a form loads to populate calculated fields or set defaults.
// Before BR: Validate before save (like EF interceptor)
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  // 'current' = the record about to be saved
  // 'previous' = the record's state before changes
  if (current.priority.changesTo(1) && !current.assignment_group) {
    current.setAbortAction(true); // Like throwing ValidationException
    gs.addErrorMessage('P1 incidents require an assignment group');
  }
})(current, previous);

Senior Considerations

  • Performance awareness: Before/After BRs are synchronous — they block the user's save like sync middleware. Keep them under 200ms. Heavy work goes to Async BRs.
  • No dependency injection: Unlike .NET where you'd inject services into filters, Business Rules access shared logic through Script Includes (ServiceNow's equivalent of utility classes/services).
  • The 'previous' object: This is gold for .NET devs — it's like EF's ChangeTracker. You can compare current.state vs previous.state to detect exactly what changed, similar to checking entity.State in EF.
💡 .NET Developer Pro Tip

If you've ever written a global action filter in ASP.NET that logs every request, you already understand Before Query Business Rules — they modify every database query on a table, like applying a global .Where() clause to every LINQ query automatically.

question: Your team lead says 'We don't write raw REST controllers in ServiceNow — we use the Table API and Scripted REST APIs.' As someone who's built hundreds of Web API controllers in .NET, explain how ServiceNow's REST story compares. When would you use Table API vs Scripted REST, and what catches developers off guard?
answer:
Why Interviewers Ask This

This tests whether you can translate your deep REST API experience into ServiceNow's two-tier API model. The key insight: ServiceNow gives you a free, auto-generated CRUD API for every table (Table API), plus the ability to build custom endpoints (Scripted REST) when you need more control.

The Direct Comparison

// ASP.NET Web API (what you've built)
[Route("api/incidents")]
public class IncidentController : ApiController {
  [HttpGet] public IEnumerable<Incident> GetAll() { ... }
  [HttpGet("{id}")] public Incident Get(string id) { ... }
  [HttpPost] public IActionResult Create(Incident model) { ... }
}

// ServiceNow Table API (auto-generated, zero code)
// GET  /api/now/table/incident              → GetAll
// GET  /api/now/table/incident/{sys_id}     → Get by ID
// POST /api/now/table/incident              → Create
// PUT  /api/now/table/incident/{sys_id}     → Update
// Every table gets this for free — no controller needed

Table API vs Scripted REST

  • Table API = Like scaffolded controllers from dotnet aspnet-codegenerator. Zero code, full CRUD, supports query parameters (sysparm_query, sysparm_fields, sysparm_limit). Perfect for standard integrations. It's the equivalent of OData endpoints in .NET — auto-exposed, filterable, paginated.
  • Scripted REST API = Like writing a custom ApiController from scratch. You define the HTTP method, path, query params, and write the processing logic. Use when Table API isn't enough — custom business logic, aggregations, multi-table joins, or non-CRUD operations.
// Scripted REST API Resource (like a .NET Controller Action)
(function process(request, response) {
  var incidentId = request.pathParams.id;
  
  // Custom logic — aggregate child tasks
  var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
  if (gr.get(incidentId)) {
    var taskCount = new GlideAggregate('task');
    taskCount.addQuery('parent', incidentId);
    taskCount.addAggregate('COUNT');
    taskCount.query();
    
    response.setBody({
      number: gr.getValue('number'),
      state: gr.getDisplayValue('state'),
      child_task_count: taskCount.next() ? 
        parseInt(taskCount.getAggregate('COUNT')) : 0
    });
  } else {
    response.setStatus(404);
    response.setBody({error: 'Incident not found'});
  }
})(request, response);

What Catches Developers Off Guard

  • No model binding: There's no [FromBody] attribute. You parse the request body manually with request.body.data — feels like Express.js more than ASP.NET.
  • ACLs still apply: Unlike .NET where you explicitly add [Authorize], ServiceNow's ACL system enforces row-level and field-level security on Table API calls by default. Your API consumer only sees records they're authorized to access.
  • Response format: Table API wraps everything in {"result": [...]}. If you're building a mobile app expecting flat JSON, Scripted REST gives you full control over the response shape.
  • Rate limiting is platform-managed: No need to implement your own throttling middleware — ServiceNow handles rate limits at the instance level.
💡 .NET Developer Pro Tip

Think of Table API as your auto-generated OData endpoints and Scripted REST as your custom ApiControllers. The decision matrix is the same: use the auto-generated path for standard CRUD, build custom when business logic demands it. Your instinct to version APIs, validate input, and return proper HTTP status codes transfers perfectly.

question: You've been managing deployments with CI/CD pipelines, Git branches, and Azure DevOps. Now someone says ServiceNow uses 'Update Sets' for version control. How would you explain Update Sets to your .NET team, what are the limitations compared to Git, and when do real-world problems occur?
answer:
What This Question Really Tests

This question reveals whether you understand that ServiceNow's deployment model is fundamentally different from code-based deployments. Update Sets track configuration changes (not source code) and move them between instances — and the limitations catch every developer coming from a Git workflow.

The Mental Model

// Git Workflow (what you know)
// feature-branch → commit → pull request → merge → CI/CD → deploy
//
// ServiceNow Update Set Workflow
// Dev Instance → Make changes (auto-captured) →
//   → Complete Update Set → Export XML →
//   → Import to Test → Preview (conflict check) →
//   → Commit → Repeat to Prod

// An Update Set is like a Git stash that auto-captures every
// config change you make while it's "In Progress"

What Transfers and What Doesn't

  • What works like Git: Changes are grouped logically (like a feature branch), they move from Dev → Test → Prod (like environments), and you can preview conflicts before committing (like merge conflict detection).
  • What breaks your Git brain: There's no branching. No diffing individual lines. No rollback to a previous commit. No pull requests or code review workflow built-in. If two developers change the same Business Rule in separate Update Sets, the last one committed wins — there's no three-way merge.

Real-World Problems

  • The 'wrong Update Set' disaster: A developer forgets to switch their active Update Set and makes changes in the wrong one. Now unrelated customizations are bundled together. In Git terms, it's like committing to main instead of your feature branch — except there's no git cherry-pick to fix it easily.
  • Collision on shared records: Two developers modify the same UI Policy. Both Update Sets capture the full record. Whichever is committed second overwrites the first entirely — no merge, no conflict resolution. The mitigation: communicate, use batch Update Sets, or use ServiceNow's newer Source Control Integration (connects to Git for scoped apps).
  • Data vs Configuration: Update Sets only capture configuration (scripts, UI policies, ACLs). They do NOT capture data (records in custom tables, user records, CMDB entries). Data migration requires separate strategies — Import Sets, scripts, or ATF data.
// Checking which Update Set you're working in (common sanity check)
var currentUS = gs.getUpdateSetName();
gs.info('Currently working in: ' + currentUS);

// Programmatically moving a record to the correct Update Set
var us = new GlideRecord('sys_update_set');
us.addQuery('name', 'My Feature Update Set');
us.addQuery('state', 'in progress');
us.query();
if (us.next()) {
  // Now switch context
  gs.setCurrentUpdate(us.sys_id);
}
💡 .NET Developer Pro Tip

ServiceNow now offers Source Control Integration for Scoped Applications — this connects to Git repositories and gives you the branch/merge/PR workflow you're used to. If you're building scoped apps, push for this approach. For global configurations, Update Sets remain the primary mechanism, so learn the discipline of checking your active Update Set before every change.

question: In ASP.NET, you separate concerns with Controllers, Services, and Repositories. In ServiceNow, there's something called 'Script Includes' that people say is like a reusable class library. But then there's also 'GlideAjax' which apparently bridges client and server. Explain the ServiceNow layered architecture to someone who thinks in MVC.
answer:
The Intent Behind This Question

This tests whether you can map ServiceNow's server-client architecture to the layered patterns you've built in .NET. The key insight: ServiceNow's UI is server-rendered (think classic ASP.NET Web Forms / Razor Pages), not a detached SPA. The client-server boundary is explicit and enforced.

The Architecture Map

// ASP.NET MVC Architecture (what you know)
//
// View (.cshtml)          → Client Scripts + UI Policies
// Controller              → Business Rules (server triggers)
// Service Layer           → Script Includes (reusable classes)
// Repository / DbContext  → GlideRecord (data access)
// AJAX calls (fetch/axios) → GlideAjax (client-to-server bridge)
// ViewComponents          → UI Scripts, Widgets (Service Portal)
// [Authorize] attribute   → ACLs (access control lists)
// Startup.cs middleware   → System Properties + Before Query BRs

Script Includes — Your Service Layer

// This is like a C# class in your Services/ folder
var IncidentHelper = Class.create();
IncidentHelper.prototype = Object.extendsObject(
  AbstractAjaxProcessor, { // Extend this to expose via GlideAjax
  
  // Server-only method (like a private service method)
  calculateSLA: function(incidentGR) {
    var priority = incidentGR.getValue('priority');
    var slaHours = {1: 4, 2: 8, 3: 24, 4: 72};
    return slaHours[priority] || 72;
  },
  
  // Client-callable method (like a [HttpGet] API endpoint)
  getIncidentSLA: function() {
    var incId = this.getParameter('sysparm_incident_id');
    var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
    if (gr.get(incId)) {
      return this.calculateSLA(gr);
    }
    return -1;
  },
  
  type: 'IncidentHelper'
});

GlideAjax — Your AJAX Calls

// Client Script calling GlideAjax
// This is like: fetch('/api/incident/getSLA?id=123')
var ga = new GlideAjax('IncidentHelper'); // The Script Include name
ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getIncidentSLA'); // Method to call
ga.addParam('sysparm_incident_id', g_form.getUniqueValue());
ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
  // 'answer' is the return value from the server method
  g_form.setValue('u_sla_hours', answer);
});

The Critical Boundary

  • Client-side (runs in browser): Client Scripts, UI Policies, UI Scripts, GlideAjax calls. You have g_form (form manipulation API — like jQuery for ServiceNow forms) and g_user (current user context).
  • Server-side (runs on instance): Business Rules, Script Includes, Scheduled Jobs, Flow Designer. You have GlideRecord, GlideSystem (gs), and full database access.
  • You cannot call GlideRecord from a Client Script. This is the #1 mistake .NET devs make — assuming they can query the DB from the browser like they would with Entity Framework in a Blazor Server app. The bridge is always GlideAjax.
💡 .NET Developer Pro Tip

Think of GlideAjax as your fetch('/api/...') calls. The Script Include with AbstractAjaxProcessor is your API Controller. The method you call via sysparm_name is the action method. The parameters you pass are your query string. Everything you know about async client-server communication applies — just with different syntax.

question: You've configured [Authorize(Roles = 'Admin')] and policy-based authorization in dozens of .NET apps. ServiceNow uses 'ACLs' — Access Control Lists — to protect data at the table, row, and field level. Walk me through how ACLs work, the evaluation order, and what surprises a developer used to role-based auth in .NET.
answer:
Why This Comes Up in Interviews

ServiceNow ACLs are a declarative security layer that evaluates automatically on every data access — UI, API, scripts, everywhere. Unlike .NET where you explicitly decorate endpoints with [Authorize], ACLs are always on. This is closer to SQL Server's row-level security or Azure AD's conditional access than ASP.NET's attribute-based auth.

Evaluation Order (Most to Least Specific)

// ACL Evaluation Hierarchy
// Think of it like CSS specificity — most specific wins
//
// 1. table.field    (e.g., incident.caller_id)     → Most specific
// 2. table.*        (e.g., incident.*)              → Table-level
// 3. *.field        (e.g., *.caller_id)             → Field across all tables
// 4. *.*            (e.g., *.*)                     → Global default
//
// Operations: read, write, create, delete
// Must pass BOTH the matching field rule AND the matching table rule.
// More-specific rules stop processing of less-specific ones, and
// several rules matching at the SAME point are OR'd (pass any one).

// .NET Equivalent Mental Model:
// [Authorize(Roles = "itil")]           → Role check in ACL
// [Authorize(Policy = "SameTeam")]      → Script/Condition in ACL
// Both must pass = AND behavior

The Three ACL Components

  • Role requirement: Like [Authorize(Roles = "itil")]. User must have the specified role.
  • Condition: A filter query on the record — like a LINQ .Where() clause. Example: active=true^assigned_to=javascript:gs.getUserID() means 'only if the record is active AND assigned to the current user.'
  • Script: Advanced logic in JavaScript. Like writing a custom IAuthorizationHandler in .NET policy-based auth. Returns true/false.
// ACL Script example — like a custom IAuthorizationHandler
// This runs on every read of the incident table
answer = (function() {
  // Allow if user is in the same department as the caller
  var caller = current.caller_id.department;
  var userDept = gs.getUser().getDepartmentID();
  return caller == userDept;
})();

What Surprises .NET Developers

  • ACLs are always enforced: Unlike .NET where forgetting [Authorize] means open access, ServiceNow denies access by default if no ACL grants it. It's a whitelist model, not a blacklist.
  • Admin bypasses everything: The admin role skips ACL evaluation entirely — unless the ACL script explicitly checks for admin. This is like having a global [AllowAnonymous] override for admins, which can be a security concern.
  • API calls respect ACLs: If you call the Table API as a service account, ACLs on that user's roles determine what's returned. There's no separate API auth layer — unlike .NET where you might have different auth for UI vs API.
  • Row + field AND catches people: If the table-level ACL requires role 'itil' AND the field-level ACL requires role 'incident_manager', the user needs BOTH roles — like stacking [Authorize] attributes. But note the flip side: multiple ACLs matching at the same point are OR'd, so passing any one of them is enough.
💡 .NET Developer Pro Tip

Enable Debug Security Rules (System Security > Debugging) in your dev instance — it's like adding app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage() for auth. You'll see exactly which ACLs evaluated, which passed, and which blocked access. Essential for debugging 'why can't this user see this record?' issues.

question: You're used to managing NuGet packages and npm modules with clear dependency trees. ServiceNow has 'Scoped Applications' and 'Global scope.' Explain the scoping model to a full-stack developer, why it matters, and what goes wrong when teams ignore it.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

ServiceNow's scoping model is its namespace and package system. It determines what code can access what data, prevents naming collisions, and controls cross-application dependencies — exactly like .NET namespaces + assembly isolation + NuGet package boundaries.

The Mental Model

// .NET Namespace / Assembly Model (what you know)
// MyCompany.HRApp (separate project/assembly)
//   → Can only access its own classes
//   → Must reference other assemblies explicitly
//   → Published as NuGet package for reuse
//
// ServiceNow Scoped Application
// x_myco_hr_app (scoped app)
//   → Can only access its own tables, scripts, BRs
//   → Must use API bridges to access global/other scopes
//   → Published to ServiceNow Store for reuse

// Global Scope = Like putting everything in one giant project
// with 'public static' on everything. Works, but no isolation.

Why It Matters

  • Table isolation: A scoped app's tables (e.g., x_myco_hr_app_request) are owned by that app. Other apps can't modify them without explicit cross-scope access. Like internal vs public in C#.
  • Script isolation: A Script Include in scope A cannot directly call a Script Include in scope B — you need cross-scope access grants. Like assembly references in .NET.
  • Update Set containment: Scoped app changes are versioned together and can be published as a single deployable unit — like packaging a NuGet library.

What Goes Wrong When Teams Ignore It

  • The 'Global scope soup' problem: Teams dump everything into Global scope. No isolation, naming collisions (two Script Includes named 'Utils'), and no way to cleanly deploy one feature without dragging unrelated changes. It's like having a .NET solution with one giant project and no separation of concerns.
  • Upgrade conflicts: Global customizations can collide with ServiceNow platform upgrades. Scoped apps are protected — the platform won't overwrite scoped artifacts during upgrades. Think of it like the difference between modifying a NuGet package's source code vs extending it through interfaces.
  • Cross-scope permission errors: Developers build in Global, then try to move to a scoped app and find their GlideRecord calls to OOB tables fail because cross-scope access isn't granted. The fix: explicitly configure 'Accessible from' in Application Access settings.
// Cross-scope access — like adding a project reference
// In a Scoped App Script Include:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident'); // OOB global table
// This FAILS unless the app's Application Access
// has 'Can read' enabled for 'incident' table

// Check current scope programmatically
var scope = gs.getCurrentScopeName();
gs.info('Running in scope: ' + scope);
// Output: 'x_myco_hr_app' or 'global'
💡 .NET Developer Pro Tip

Treat scoped applications like microservices — each owns its data, exposes APIs for others, and is independently deployable. Start every new project as a scoped app, not in Global. Your future self (and the upgrade team) will thank you. The discipline is identical to keeping your .NET solution modular.

question: You've set up hundreds of automated CI/CD tests in xUnit and NUnit. Your ServiceNow team mentions 'ATF' — Automated Test Framework. How does it compare to your .NET testing experience, and what kind of testing does ServiceNow handle that's fundamentally different from unit testing code?
answer:
Reading Between the Lines

ATF (Automated Test Framework) is ServiceNow's built-in testing platform. But unlike xUnit/NUnit which test code in isolation, ATF tests platform behavior — form loads, workflow executions, security rules, and UI interactions. It's closer to Selenium + integration testing than pure unit testing.

The Comparison

// .NET Testing Pyramid (what you know)
// Unit Tests (xUnit)     → Test individual methods/classes
// Integration Tests      → Test API endpoints, DB operations
// E2E Tests (Selenium)   → Test full UI workflows
//
// ServiceNow ATF Maps To:
// Server-side steps      → Integration tests (BR fires correctly)
// Form-based steps       → E2E tests (form loads, fields populate)
// Flow/Workflow steps    → Integration tests (automation works)
// Security steps         → Auth tests (ACLs enforce correctly)
// No pure unit testing   → Script Includes tested via server steps

What ATF Handles That's Different

  • Configuration testing: Did the UI Policy hide the right field? Does the Business Rule auto-populate the correct value? These aren't code tests — they're platform behavior tests. No equivalent in .NET because you write the behavior; in ServiceNow, you configure it.
  • Impersonation: ATF can run tests as different users to verify role-based access — like having test fixtures that swap identity mid-test. Run as User: helpdesk.agent → verify they can create incidents but can't delete them.
  • Parameterized test suites: Group ATF tests into suites that run against specific Update Sets before deployment — like a gate in your Azure DevOps pipeline. This is how mature ServiceNow teams prevent regressions.
// ATF Test Step Example — Server-side Script step
// (like writing an xUnit [Fact] method)
(function(outputs, steps, params, stepResult, assertEqual) {
  // Arrange: Create a test incident
  var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
  gr.initialize();
  gr.short_description = 'ATF Test Incident';
  gr.impact = 1;
  gr.urgency = 1;
  gr.insert();
  
  // Act: Re-query to check Business Rule fired
  gr.get(gr.sys_id);
  
  // Assert: Priority should be auto-calculated to 1 (Critical)
  assertEqual({
    name: 'Priority auto-calculated',
    shouldbe: '1',
    value: gr.getValue('priority')
  });
  
  // Cleanup
  gr.deleteRecord();
})(outputs, steps, params, stepResult, assertEqual);

Limitations vs .NET Testing

  • No mocking framework: You can't mock GlideRecord calls like you'd mock IRepository with Moq. Tests hit real tables.
  • No TDD workflow: ATF tests are created in the UI, not in an IDE. The feedback loop is slower than dotnet test --watch.
  • Test data management: ATF creates real records during tests. Cleanup is manual unless you build it into your test steps.
💡 .NET Developer Pro Tip

Think of ATF as your integration test suite with Selenium-like capabilities built in. Use it for regression testing before deployments — especially for Business Rules, ACLs, and Flows. For Script Include logic, write ATF server-side steps that exercise the methods directly, similar to calling service methods in integration tests.
